analysis.one_liner: Imposes a one-time 14.25% tax on personal net worth above $10 million to pay down national debt.
analysis.headline: A one-time 14.25% tax on wealth above $10 million was introduced by a single House Democrat with zero cosponsors and has sat in committee, with no hearing or vote, since April 2026.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would charge every U.S. citizen or resident household and trust a one-time tax of 14.25% on whatever their net worth exceeds $10 million, counting everything they own as of the day the bill passes except their primary home and its mortgage. The bill's stated goal is paying down the roughly $30 trillion national debt. It is framed around a one-time wealth tax Donald Trump himself proposed as a presidential candidate in 1999, quoting his statements and debt warnings from Republican leaders to argue the idea has bipartisan roots.
analysis.who_benefits: If enacted, all federal taxpayers would benefit from whatever debt reduction the tax produced — the bill's own findings claim a $5.7 trillion raise would cut the debt-to-GDP ratio from about 101% to 83% [S2]. Households with less than $10 million in net worth would pay nothing, since the tax only applies above that threshold and exempts the primary residence [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a one-time 14.25% tax on the portion of an applicable taxpayer's net worth above $10 million, measured on the date of enactment, with the primary residence and its mortgage excluded from the calculation.
Applies to U.S. citizens and residents and to the portions of domestic and foreign trusts benefiting U.S. citizens or residents, which limits the ability to shelter wealth in trusts.

The bill's findings argue that if the tax raised the $5.7 trillion Trump expected of his 1999 plan, it would lower the debt-to-GDP ratio from roughly 101% to 83%, easing a fiscal burden the bill quotes Republican leaders calling a threat to future generations.

analysis.who_pays: Individuals, and trusts benefiting U.S. persons, whose net worth (excluding their home) exceeds $10 million would owe a one-time payment of 14.25% of everything above that line — a group numbering in the tens of thousands of households holding most measured U.S. wealth. Owners of illiquid assets such as private businesses would owe tax on paper value they cannot easily convert to cash.

drawbacks.text: A tax on total net worth hits illiquid assets: an owner of a valuable private business or farmland could owe 14.25% of paper value without the cash to pay it, and the bill exempts only the primary residence, not working assets.

The claimed $5.7 trillion in revenue is not an independent estimate — it is the figure Donald Trump gave for his own 1999 proposal, quoted in the bill's findings — and the bill has never been scored by the Congressional Budget Office.

Every asset in the country above the threshold would need a fair-market valuation on a single date, inviting disputes and litigation over hard-to-price holdings like private companies, art, and partnership stakes.

The bill names a sitting political figure in its title and builds its findings around his old statements, marking it as a political message rather than a negotiated policy; it drew zero cosponsors, including from members who otherwise back wealth taxes.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: On paper the trade is favorable to ordinary people: a one-time levy confined to the wealthiest households in exchange for meaningful national debt reduction, with homes shielded. But the design is rough — it taxes illiquid wealth people cannot easily pay from, its revenue claim rests on a 27-year-old campaign estimate rather than an official score, and its zero cosponsors and single-date net-worth snapshot make enactment, in anything like this form, practically impossible.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee has taken no further action — no hearing, no vote — with the Congress running until January 3, 2027.

narrative.text: Rep. Juan Vargas introduced the bill on April 15, 2026, and it was referred the same day to the House Ways and Means Committee, the panel that writes tax law.
No cosponsors signed on and the committee has taken no action since referral, leaving the bill with no path to a floor vote unless that changes.

The bill's text and findings are built as an argument from Donald Trump's own 1999 wealth tax proposal and Republican statements on the national debt, rather than as a compromise or a scaled-down measure.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Households with more than $10 million in net worth, who face no new tax and were never seriously threatened by a bill that attracted no cosponsors or committee action.

for.name: Rep. Juan Vargas
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and made the case for it in its findings, quoting Trump's 1999 wealth tax plan and Republican debt warnings.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee (Chair Jason Smith)
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over all tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day of introduction and has held no hearing, markup, or vote on it.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: No floor action of any kind has been scheduled on the bill, which with zero cosponsors has no demonstrated support to compel one.

sides.party_line_note: There have been no votes and no cosponsors, so no partisan split can be measured; the only recorded actor is one Democrat, and the Republican-controlled committee has simply not acted.

industries.industry: Households and trusts with net worth over $10 million
industries.note: The bill's entire purpose is a one-time 14.25% charge on these households' wealth above $10 million, homes excluded. Their interest is in the bill never moving; the public's stated interest is the debt reduction the money would buy.

industries.industry: Wealth management, trust, and valuation services
industries.note: A one-time national valuation of every large estate would generate substantial paid valuation, appraisal, and compliance work, even as the underlying tax reduces the client assets these firms manage.

analysis.trajectory: With zero cosponsors, no committee hearing, and a House majority that has shown no interest, this will almost certainly die quietly in the Ways and Means Committee when this Congress ends on January 3, 2027 — its value to the sponsor is the recorded statement, not the tax.
